common_name: Simmonds Avocado (Historic Florida West Indian Avocado)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil well away from structures, as Simmonds grows into a large, upright tree; it is a Type A flowering cultivar, so pairing with a Type B avocado such as Choquette improves fruit set.

directions: Simmonds is one of the oldest named Florida avocado cultivars, a West Indian race selection from the Miami area that helped establish South Florida's dooryard and commercial avocado culture in the early twentieth century. It bears large, glossy green, thin-skinned fruit with mild, buttery, relatively low-oil flesh typical of West Indian parentage, ripening early in the season during mid- to late summer. As a true West Indian type it has essentially no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, frost-free conditions, but it tolerates the humid, high-rainfall summers of the Gulf Coast better than California-bred Guatemalan cultivars. Provide deep, well-drained soil and avoid overwatering, since avocado roots are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in heavy or poorly drained ground.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Avocado Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun with plenty of room to spread; Pollock is a Type A flowering West Indian cultivar best paired with a Type B avocado for reliable pollination.

directions: Pollock is among the earliest named avocado cultivars grown commercially in South Florida, a West Indian race selection prized for producing some of the largest fruit of any dooryard avocado, frequently exceeding a pound and a half. The smooth green skin encloses pale, mild, watery-textured flesh with low oil content, characteristic of pure West Indian heritage, and fruit ripens early, generally in mid- to late summer. Because it has no meaningful cold hardiness, Pollock is best suited to true tropical and near-tropical dooryards rather than the colder margins of zone 9. Give it deep, well-aerated soil and consistent moisture during fruit development, but avoid waterlogging, which quickly promotes root rot.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Avocado Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in a spacious, well-drained site; Trapp is a Type A flowering cultivar and one of the first avocados grown commercially in Florida groves.

directions: Trapp was one of the first avocado cultivars planted commercially in Miami-Dade County in the early 1900s and helped launch Florida's avocado industry decades before Lula and Waldin became standard. It produces medium to large, rounded, glossy green fruit with pale, mild, buttery flesh typical of the West Indian race, ripening in the fall, later than Simmonds or Pollock. The tree is vigorous and long-lived but, like other West Indian types, has virtually no frost tolerance and needs a warm, sheltered, frost-free site. Maintain deep mulch and well-drained soil, since avocado trees decline quickly in wet feet or compacted ground.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Booth 7 is a Type B flowering hybrid cultivar developed in Homestead, Florida and does best paired with a Type A avocado nearby.

directions: Booth 7 is a Guatemalan x West Indian hybrid bred in the historic Homestead, Florida avocado district, valued for combining better cold tolerance and richer flavor than pure West Indian cultivars with reasonably good adaptation to Florida's wet, humid summers. Fruit is medium-sized, pear-shaped, with moderately high oil content and a nutty flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. It is a somewhat more compact, precocious tree than the old West Indian heritage cultivars, making it a practical choice for dooryard growers wanting improved flavor without excessive tree size. Provide full sun and sharply drained soil, and avoid heavy irrigation once fruit begins to mature.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Avocado Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Booth 8 is a Type B flowering hybrid, a sibling selection to Booth 7 with a slightly later harvest window.

directions: Booth 8 shares its Guatemalan x West Indian parentage with Booth 7 and was selected from the same Homestead, Florida breeding program, but it ripens somewhat later in the fall and holds well on the tree once mature. The medium, pear-shaped fruit has thicker skin than many Florida cultivars, which makes it more forgiving to handle and ship, along with moderately rich, nutty flesh. It combines better disease tolerance in humid conditions than pure Guatemalan cultivars with more cold hardiness than pure West Indian types, making it a solid dual-purpose dooryard choice. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage and avoid letting the root zone stay wet for extended periods.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Avocado Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil with room to spread; Hall is a Type A flowering hybrid and a longtime staple of South Florida avocado groves.

directions: Hall is a Guatemalan x West Indian hybrid that has long been one of the more widely planted commercial and dooryard avocados in South Florida, valued for a productive, fairly reliable bearing habit. Fruit is medium to large and pear-shaped with somewhat rough, dark green skin and rich, nutty flesh with moderate oil content, ripening in fall. The tree tolerates Florida's humid summer rains better than pure Guatemalan cultivars while carrying noticeably better flavor than the older pure West Indian selections. Site it in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, and thin overly heavy fruit loads if limbs show signs of breaking.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Avocado Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in a large, open site; Monroe is a Type B flowering hybrid known for extending the home avocado harvest into winter, so pair with a Type A cultivar such as Simmonds or Hall.

directions: Monroe is a vigorous Guatemalan x West Indian hybrid grown in South Florida chiefly for its very late harvest, with large, round fruit typically maturing in early winter after most other cultivars have finished. The thick, leathery skin protects moderately oily, rich-flavored flesh that holds well after picking, and the tree's late timing makes it a useful complement to earlier-ripening cultivars like Simmonds or Choquette in a home planting. Its size makes it best suited to larger properties, and like other Guatemalan-influenced hybrids it tolerates a bit more cool weather than pure West Indian types, though it still cannot take frost. Grow in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Avocado Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Haden is the historic parent cultivar behind much of Florida's mango industry and needs a warm, frost-free site with room to grow large.

directions: Haden was grown from a seed of the Indian cultivar Mulgoba in Coconut Grove, Florida, in the early twentieth century and became the parent or grandparent of many of the mango cultivars grown in Florida today. It bears medium to large fruit with a striking yellow skin heavily blushed crimson-red, and juicy, moderately fibrous flesh with a rich, aromatic flavor when fully ripe. The tree tends toward alternate bearing and is more susceptible to anthracnose in humid weather than newer commercial cultivars, so good air circulation and a dry bloom period improve fruit set. Reduce irrigation as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate sugars, and protect the tree from any frost, since mango wood is easily damaged by cold.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes
California Rare Fruit Growers

common_name: Tommy Atkins Mango (Widely Grown Commercial Florida Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil with plenty of room; Tommy Atkins is a vigorous, highly productive Florida-origin cultivar grown commercially worldwide.

directions: Tommy Atkins is a Florida-origin seedling selection that became the most widely planted commercial mango cultivar in the world thanks to its heavy, reliable bearing and unusually good resistance to anthracnose and rough handling during shipping. The fruit is large with a strikingly showy skin blushed red, orange, and yellow, but the flesh is moderately fibrous and milder in flavor than heirloom cultivars like Haden or Carrie. Growers in humid Gulf Coast climates appreciate its disease tolerance, though home gardeners prioritizing eating quality often prefer pairing it with a richer-flavored cultivar. Give the tree full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a large, vigorous canopy unless it is pruned regularly after harvest.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Kent is a large, vigorous Florida cultivar prized for eating quality and needs generous space to mature.

directions: Kent originated in Florida in the mid-twentieth century and is regarded as one of the best-flavored large commercial mango cultivars, with rich, sweet, nearly fiberless flesh that has made it a favorite among mango connoisseurs. The large fruit has greenish-yellow skin with a red-purple blush and ripens later in the season than Haden or Tommy Atkins, extending the summer harvest. The tree is vigorous and productive, tending toward alternate bearing in some years, and benefits from post-harvest pruning to control its size and encourage new fruiting wood. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and protect from frost, as mango wood is killed by even brief freezes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil with ample room to mature; Keitt is one of the latest-ripening major Florida cultivars, extending the mango season into late summer and early fall.

directions: Keitt was selected in the Homestead, Florida mango district and is notable for ripening very late in the season, often into September, well after most other major cultivars have finished. The large fruit stays green even at full ripeness, with little or no red blush, and its flesh is sweet, juicy, and largely fiberless, making it a favorite for fresh eating. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its late timing makes it a valuable addition alongside earlier cultivars like Haden or Tommy Atkins to extend a home harvest. Provide full sun, well-drained soil, and protection from frost, since mango wood is easily damaged by cold.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Irwin is a Florida-origin cultivar that grows into a moderately compact tree compared to Kent or Tommy Atkins.

directions: Irwin originated in the Miami area and, although developed in Florida, became especially popular in Asian mango-growing regions for its deep red, glossy skin and moderately compact tree habit. The small to medium fruit has mild, sweet, only lightly fibrous flesh and ripens relatively early in the season, making it a useful complement to later Florida cultivars. Its smaller stature compared to Kent or Tommy Atkins makes it somewhat easier to manage in a dooryard setting or large container. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, reduce watering as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor, and protect the tree from frost.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Edward is an old Florida heirloom mango grown chiefly by home gardeners and small nurseries for its outstanding flavor.

directions: Edward is a mid-twentieth-century Florida-origin mango cultivar valued by home gardeners for producing rich, sweet, nearly fiberless flesh considered by many to rank among the best-tasting Florida mangoes, though it has never been grown commercially at the scale of Tommy Atkins or Kent. Fruit is medium-sized with yellow-green skin lightly blushed with red, and it ripens in mid-summer. The tree is moderately vigorous and benefits from a warm, sunny, well-drained site and occasional pruning after harvest to maintain a manageable size. Protect the tree from frost, since mango wood is damaged by even brief cold exposure.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

common_name: Van Dyke Mango (Compact Florida Dooryard Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container; Van Dyke's semi-compact habit and consistent bearing make it a popular home-garden mango in South Florida.

directions: Van Dyke is a Florida-origin mango cultivar known for its semi-compact growth habit and dependable, consistent annual bearing, qualities that made it a long-standing favorite among South Florida dooryard growers. The small to medium fruit has deep red-orange skin and moderately fibrous, sweet flesh, ripening in mid-summer. Its smaller stature relative to full-size commercial cultivars makes it a reasonable option for gardeners with limited space or for large container culture in zone 9. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness, and protect the tree from any frost.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container; Zill is a compact, early-bearing cultivar bred by South Florida's noted Zill nursery family.

directions: Zill was developed by the well-known Zill nursery family of Boynton Beach, Florida, and is valued for its compact tree size, precocious and consistent bearing, and early ripening relative to most other Florida cultivars. The small to medium fruit has deep red skin and mild, sweet, moderately fibrous flesh. Its smaller, more manageable stature makes it a practical choice for home gardens with limited space or for container growing in cooler parts of zone 9. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and protect the tree from frost, since mango wood is damaged by even brief cold snaps.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Palmer is a vigorous Florida-origin cultivar that can be kept compact with regular post-harvest pruning.

directions: Palmer originated in South Florida in the mid-twentieth century and became a popular commercial cultivar for its distinctive elongated fruit with a deep wine-red to purple blush and its consistent, heavy bearing. The flesh is mild, sweet, and moderately fibrous, and fruit ripens mid- to late season, filling a harvest window between earlier cultivars like Haden and later ones like Keitt. The tree is naturally vigorous but responds well to pruning after harvest, which keeps it manageable in a dooryard setting. Provide full sun and well-drained soil, and protect the tree from frost, since mango wood is easily killed by cold.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes
